alt: Wrapping hides a gift, marks it as a gift and signals the giver's effort. Rixom et al. (2020) found a neatly wrapped gift from a friend raised expectations so the gift was liked less, while sloppy wrapping set low expectations that the gift exceeded. Givers believe elaborate wrapping increases appreciation; Howard (1992) proposed wrapping creates a positive mood. Types range from none to boxes, neat to untidy.
caption: Neat wrapping can backfire by raising expectations the gift must meet.

alt: A two-by-two schematic of yoghurt pots: angular or rounded, high or low colour saturation, with angular and highly saturated giving the strongest expected taste. Study card: participants rated expectations, tasted yoghurt and rated intensity; angular shapes and saturated colours led to stronger taste ratings, most for those who value visual design.
caption: Angular, strongly coloured pots made the yoghurt seem more intense.

alt: An illustrative shelf display with an attention hot spot over the horizontal centre. Centre products get more visual attention, attention to the centre rises just before the choice, and central products are chosen more often. Planograms fix where products sit; a limitation is that looking is not buying.
caption: Attention drifts to the horizontal centre just before people choose.

alt: Disrupt-then-reframe: an odd price of 300 pennies briefly confuses, the reframe "that's $3, it's a bargain" resolves it, and sales increased. Kardes et al. (2007) linked it to need for cognitive closure: time pressure, fatigue and noise raise the need, and people high in it grab the reframe because it ends the confusion.
caption: Confuse, then offer an easy answer: it works best on tired, hurried buyers.

alt: Six cards: reciprocity (a free sample creates obligation), commitment and consistency (a small agreement leads to a larger one), social proof (others are buying it), liking (we agree with people we like), authority (an expert recommends it) and scarcity (only a few left).
caption: Six principles, each a different reason to say yes.

alt: The Engel Kollat Blackwell model runs through problem recognition, information search (internal or external), evaluation of alternatives, purchase and post-purchase outcomes. Post-purchase dissonance is the conflict between "I chose this" and "the rejected option had good features"; it is greater for expensive, important, hard-to-reverse purchases and attractive alternatives, and reduced by seeking supporting information, playing down the rejected option or returning the item.
caption: Dissonance follows the purchase and is worst for costly, hard-to-reverse choices.
